dataset.name: aisi-tracker
dataset.title: AI Security Institutes tracker
dataset.description: Which states have an AI Security Institute (AISI), covering all 193 UN member states plus Taiwan and the EU AI Office, with funding, staff and leadership where published. Every record cites its sources.
dataset.definition: We count a body as an AI Security Institute (AISI) if a national government, or the EU, has tasked it with testing general-purpose or frontier AI models for their capabilities and risks, or has named it its AI safety institute or its AI security institute. A regulator, certification body or cyber security agency does not count for that role alone.
dataset.license_note: Quotations from sources remain with their rights holders and are reproduced as quotations; the licence covers our own compilation, text and data.
dataset.citation: Accelerate Europe (2026). AI Security Institutes tracker, version 1.0.1, data as of 24 October 2026. Compiled by Jason Hoelscher-Obermaier. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23600431
dataset.scope: Status is tracked for all 193 UN member states, Taiwan (as a territory) and the EU AI Office. The Europe page counts the 27 EU member states, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, the United Kingdom and Switzerland.

method.text: Qualifying body. A government act either (a) designates the body as the state's AI safety or AI security institute in the sense of the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes), as its member institution in that Network, or as the state's counterpart to other AI safety institutes (a body, not a ministry desk); or (b) assigns it, as a national public function, the evaluation or testing of general-purpose, foundation or frontier AI models for their capabilities or for risks arising from the model's own capabilities or behaviour, such as misuse potential, harmful outputs or loss of control. Assignment means a constitutive or mandate decision, or an authorised announcement of an ongoing public responsibility. A research programme, funding line, testing schedule, rename, government support or recognition, the state's Network membership, or the body's own description is not an assignment. Title, legal form, newness and size do not matter. These do not qualify a body on their own: certifying products or deployed systems, conformity assessment, market surveillance (including AI Act authorities; Spain's planned institute inside AESIA shows how such an authority can host one), securing AI systems against attack (for example prompt-injection hardening or security certification), auditing fairness, bias, explainability or trustworthiness, performance benchmarking, general AI research or R&D networks, promotion and sandboxes. Ladder. Each state's status is the strongest act in force concerning a qualifying body, dated from that act. Established: an official text says the body exists or has been designated. A body announced as established counts before it operates; known activity is reported separately. Planned: an adopted commitment to create or designate a named qualifying body, through a cabinet or council decision, an adopted strategy or plan naming it, an enacted budget line, or a statement by the head of government or responsible minister. Proposed: the government's own formal proposal awaiting approval, submitted to cabinet or parliament or published by the responsible ministry for formal consultation. Exploring: the government studies the option of a qualifying body or promises a report on it; an internal or working draft names one; or a government-appointed advisory commission publishes a recommendation that itself names a qualifying body or function. Generic AI institutes, centres or councils, and exploring a lab, network or mechanism without a qualifying remit, do not count. Parliamentary and independent inquiries do not count. Rejection, withdrawal, lapse or supersession returns the state to 'None identified' unless another act qualifies; silence is not rejection. Signing an international statement such as the Seoul statement of intent, or joining the Network, does not count by itself. Dates and precision. Use a year-only date when no exact date is published. If the creation date is not published, use only supported precision and state the limit. A record may use the first retrieved official confirmation, clearly identified as confirmation rather than the founding date.

Why this bar: evaluating advanced AI models is what distinguishes an AISI from AI regulators and digital ministries, and it is the work members of the international network do together. Budgets and staff differ too much between countries for a size threshold to work, so we report them separately, together with whether published work is credited to the institute.

How each state was checked: 'individual' means the sources for that state were searched and read one by one; 'broad search' means it was covered only by searches across many countries, so 'None identified' is weaker evidence there.
Population of European states: Eurostat, 1 January 2025. 'Under 10 million' on the page means fewer than 10 million people.

Missing values: an omitted field or null means not known or not published, never zero or false. For budget and staff, Not published means that no figure was found in the sources checked; these searches are not yet logged with dates, unlike those for testing and access.

Population outside the 32 European states: World Bank, latest available year; Taiwan: its Ministry of the Interior. Regions: the UN's standard country grouping (M49). The UN does not list Taiwan separately, so we place it in Eastern Asia.

Known activity: assessed separately from government status and shown only for established institutes. Published work is a published evaluation, test result, benchmark or technical report credited to the institute by name, including named organisational contributions and documented predecessors. Joint testing is named participation in a testing exercise; an exercise is classified as joint testing even when the institute also authors its report. Guidance alone, policy or programme reports, country-only or host-agency credit, and staff affiliations alone do not qualify. Tools, datasets and benchmarks qualify only as evaluation artefacts. Every output records its qualification and reason. Each kind uses its earliest qualifying institute-credit date, retaining the recorded precision and citing that item. No qualifying work means none was found. Absence is not evidence of inactivity.

Freshness: the recorded check date is the last full re-check of a record. Reading some sources, checking identifiers or adding excerpts does not advance it. Partial work is recorded separately with its date and scope. Historical dates whose original full-check logs are unavailable are marked historical upper bounds; these do not guarantee freshness.

Rescinded or replaced instruments: records describe the current state, and a fact resting on a rescinded or replaced instrument never appears as current. History is kept only where the instrument is itself a recorded act (a timeline event, legal basis, name or agreement), dated with the date it was rescinded and the act that rescinded it, both sourced. Context or supporting notes resting on a replaced instrument are removed, not annotated. Sources that are legal instruments carry the date their status was last verified; record checks re-verify it, and the release check warns when a cited instrument's status was last verified more than six months before release.

Status confidence measures evidence, not disagreement over classification: high means a primary source states the decisive act; medium means indirect primary evidence or several independent secondary accounts; low means a single secondary source. For a finding of no institute, medium requires an individual check with recorded queries in English and a national or official language, plus at least one retrieved primary source showing the state's AI governance set-up, consistent with no qualifying institute. English meets both language requirements where it is official; the language note records the languages searched and coverage limits. The governance citations and note identify the reviewed governance evidence. English-only searches where English is not official, secondary-only evidence and other incomplete checks remain low. High additionally requires a dated official primary statement, no more than 12 calendar months before the dataset date, explicitly saying no institute exists or is planned. Medium has no fixed age limit; original search and full-check dates show freshness. This finding is limited to our search; it is not proof of absence.

Excerpts: every positive status, status date, legal basis, budget amount, staff figure, first output, agreement, head, reporting line, partner relation and partner how sentence needs a short quotation that carries the claim. Other fields have excerpts where possible. Each gloss translates only its own excerpt and adds no facts. Each quotation is linked to the values it supports; a check confirms each link exists, and review judges whether the quotation supports the value.

Outputs: a publication, tool or dataset counts when it is written by the institute or credited to it as its own work, including named organisational contributions. Publishing or hosting alone does not count when the institute acts only as a regulator or facilitator for work drafted by others. Commissioned work published as the institute's own publication counts, with the research author identified. Staff co-authorship or a link in a staff bibliography alone does not count. Host-agency and government documents count only when the institute is named as author. Translations of other bodies' documents do not count. Drafts, versions, summaries and translations within one document lineage form one item, with the latest title and the earliest public date. Documented former names and institutional predecessors follow the same credit rule; their inclusion does not backdate government designation. Every catalogue output records an explicit institutional credit identity and date. The catalogue date is shared across a document lineage; the credit date records the earliest public version for which the institute’s credit is supported. If institute credit first appears in a later version, its credit date is later than the lineage date. An institute's own later post does not backdate that credit to an earlier staff-only paper. An explicit official retrospective statement naming the institute as author or crediting the earlier version as its own work can establish credit for that version; a statement that it merely published or hosted the work cannot. For arXiv papers, the recorded first-submission date is used as the bibliographic version date; it does not establish the exact day that the paper became publicly accessible. Cite the artefact itself where it can be retrieved.

First output: the earliest qualifying date credited to the institute by name, including network reports that name it. Use the explicitly recorded institutional credit date. It is not limited to evaluations. Country or host-agency participation alone does not name an institute.

Intervals between milestones are computed from recorded dates, never entered by hand. They are counted in signed whole days: from announcement to establishment, from establishment to the first qualifying activity, and from announcement to the first qualifying activity. Announcement is read from the commitment and proposal events in the timeline and establishment from the designations that have not been withdrawn. A designation is never read as an announcement, so a state designated without an earlier recorded commitment or proposal has no announcement interval. The first qualifying activity is the earliest institute-credit date of any output that qualifies as Known activity, including work credited to documented predecessors. It dates the first documented qualifying credit, which can be later than the work itself; participants in one joint exercise share that date when their credit begins with the same public version. It is not the generated first output, which also counts guidance and other outputs that do not qualify. The two activity intervals are given only while the institute is established, even where qualifying work is credited to a planned or proposed body. A month-only or year-only date is read as every day of that month or year up to the dataset date, never as a midpoint, so the interval is a range from its shortest to its longest reading. Where several records could mark a milestone, it runs from the earliest day any of them can mean to the earliest day by which one of them certainly happened. A negative interval means the later milestone came first; a range from a negative to a positive value means the order is not known. An interval is empty when either date is not recorded. The intervals are not a measure of speed or quality: the announcing act and the kind of body differ between states, for example a rename of an existing body, a federation of existing bodies, a new agency, or one legal act with separate adoption and entry-into-force dates.

Agreements: the institute must be a named party to the agreement, or a government agreement must name it as an implementing body. A signed agreement requires a signatory; an announced agreement must identify the intended institute party or implementing role. A pledge records a company commitment announced by the government for the institute or its documented predecessor, with no signed agreement established; a recipient is the beneficiary of that commitment. An institute can be a named agreement party or a named implementer of a government agreement. Only pledges record recipients. States describe the recorded act, not proof that its original terms remain in force. Where an agreement names possible collaboration, its scope preserves that condition. Purely domestic inter-agency memorandums do not count. The institute counterparty type is reserved for peer AI Security Institutes and the EU AI Office; other research organisations use other.

Annual funding: every amount with a stated funding year or period has an annual amount and an explanation of its basis, including supplementary, proposed, related-body and press-reported amounts. Preserve the commitment, scope and confidence label; an annual figure is not proof of adoption or expenditure. Use the allocation for the fiscal year containing the dataset date when a yearly profile is published. Otherwise use a mean over a stated multi-year duration, or the nominal amount for a single stated funding year, and explain its basis. One-off supplementary amounts are attributed to their funding year, not treated as recurring spending. The annual basis distinguishes current-year allocations, period means and other figures. A launch or announcement year alone is not a funding period; do not invent an annual figure when no period is stated. For comparison, the reference year is the calendar year of the dataset date. Compare only a whole-institute annual figure, adopted or announced, whose funding period overlaps the reference year; one-off amounts are never compared. Among several, prefer the period containing the dataset date, then the latest earlier period, then the nearest later period; for equal periods prefer adopted, then the latest decision. Proposals and periods outside the reference year are never compared. Components are never compared alone. A published annual allocation takes precedence over a period mean for the same date. Component quotations support the inputs to a calculated total, not a quotation of the result. Decisions dated wholly after the dataset date are excluded from comparison; partial decision dates retain their recorded precision.

AI Act authorities: an act in force takes precedence over an inconsistent Commission list. Every EU or EEA authority record also cites the Commission list. The designation basis records a law, decree, government decision, cabinet decision, ministerial act or the absence of an identified act; where no national designation act is identified, the basis is recorded as not yet identified. A pending proposal is not a designation in force. For the listed uses, Article 74(8) requires every member state to designate either its competent data protection supervisory authorities or another authority meeting the stated independence conditions; it does not automatically designate data protection authorities in all member states.

Leadership: a head is stated only when an official channel of the institute, its host or its government names the person in the role, such as its website, a government directory or an official social account. Press reports alone do not qualify. Otherwise the row reads not published; not applicable is used only where no institute exists. The role title is the exact published one; if none is published, the role is recorded as lead with a note that no formal title is published. The head is the top executive by published title, the chair excluded, and "Acting" and "part-time" are kept as published. The newest official source wins and a conflict is noted. A historical appointment or signature does not by itself confirm continuing tenure.

Reporting line: the body an institute reports to is the ministry-level body the sources place it under: one above an agency, university or research host, and the host itself when the host is a ministry. Several bodies are joined with "; ". The excerpt carries the source's own wording and nothing is inferred; where no text names a parent, the row is not published.

National partners: a partner is a domestic public body or public-interest research organisation that a primary text of the institute or its government names as working with the institute on its mission. The host, funders of the host, private firms, catch-all groups and the reports-to body are never entries. A consortium is one entry, and its members are listed individually only with separate evidence. Member is used only when the institute is a federation of existing bodies and the text lists the body as a constituent. Works with is used when a text in force assigns the body a specific task with the institute; an adopted programme for the current period that assigns the work counts as in force. Planned is used when the text is a plan, strategy or future commitment. A body named only as an example in a general duty to cooperate is not entered. The cyber agency flag marks the national cyber security agency or the body containing it; when no entry has the flag, the notes name the cyber agency searched and the date, and no other absence is ever claimed. What says in two to six words what the body is, from its own page or the quote. How is one sentence of at most 25 words written from the bound quote alone, like a gloss. Every stated value, relation and how is bound to a verbatim excerpt; not published needs the dated search log. The card shows six partners, cyber agency first, then members, works with, planned, then in authored order; the rest are in the card's "How they work together" fold and in the downloads and the API.

Testing capacity and model access: each institute records whether a source states that it tests AI models and how it gets access to them, using only the defined codes. Every value other than not published needs a verbatim excerpt from a retrieved source in which the institute, or a body explicitly acting for it, is the subject. Never infer a value from press narrative, a parent ministry's powers, a partner's general expertise or network membership. Testing capacity may hold one or both modes. In house: a source reports testing or evaluation of AI models that the institute itself has carried out or is carrying out, such as published results, a network report crediting it with running tests, or an official statement that it is already testing; a statement of role, function or focus does not count. For a federation, only testing that a source attributes to the institute counts, never a member body's own general track record. A joint network testing report counts as the institute's own testing only if it says the institute ran tests, not only analysis, translation checks or task design, and the institute existed at that date. Via other bodies: a source states that a named body outside the institute, such as a contractor or partner lab, tests or evaluates models for it. Model access records what sources state, and its value is derived from that, never set by hand. An access event is dated access by the institute to a model before its public release, or deeper than the public gets, such as reduced or removed safeguards, weights or internals; testing through a public interface is not an event, and testing alone shows access only if the source says the developer gave it. An event's date is the model's public release date unless the date of the access is published; either way it is the date by which access had happened, so the access took place on or before it. An event counts when the model is in Epoch AI's frontier set, which Epoch AI defines as models in the top 5 by training compute at the time of their release, or when its developer was a leading developer at the event date: it has had a model in Epoch AI's frontier set released since 1 January 2023, and a model in Epoch AI's notable models released in the twelve months before the event. Both are cited from Epoch AI's data. Access to other models goes in the notes. A legal power is an operative provision, named by act and article, that gives the institute, or explicitly the institute on behalf of its authority, a power to require access to models, with its conditions; an explainer is not enough, the provision itself is quoted. A developer agreement is a published agreement between the institute and a developer with a model in Epoch AI's frontier set that provides for access to, or evaluation of, the developer's models. The value is Yes when the latest event falls within the twelve months up to the data date, a date known only to the month or year counting from its first possible day; Yes, evidence from the year of the latest event when it is older; otherwise By law with a legal power, Access agreed with a developer agreement, and None found with a dated search log. Planned, for testing capacity when no mode is stated: adopted text, such as a cabinet decision, an adopted plan, strategy or guidelines or a government action plan, sets it up in the future. A proposal, such as a consultation draft, a budget proposal not yet voted or a bill, gives not published, with the proposal quoted in the notes with its source and date. Not published: searched and no source states it; a dated search log records each query, its language and the sources read. Where a newer official source contradicts an older one, the newer one decides and the notes record both. Notes also record explicit negative statements, such as no own staff, and joint network testing as testing reported with its date. Not published means not stated in the sources searched, never that the institute lacks the capacity or access.

Staffing model: each institute records how a source says it is staffed, using only the defined codes; dated headcounts stay in the staff figures. Every value other than not published needs a verbatim excerpt from a retrieved source in which the institute, or a body explicitly acting for it, is the subject. Only a source published in 2023 or later supports the value, because staffing is a current arrangement and the first institutes were set up in late 2023; a page that carries no date counts as of the day it was read, and older sources go in the notes as history. Never infer a value from a legal form, a host body's own staff, a partner's expertise or press narrative. The codes are decided in this order, and the first that applies is used. Staff of existing bodies: the institute is a federation of existing bodies whose staff do its work; used only for that legal form. Core team with partner institutions: partner institutions do the institute's research or testing under its programme, such as partner cells, funded institutes or commissioned projects, and any central team of its own only coordinates, sets policy or represents it. Unit in a host body: the institute is a unit of an agency, public research body or university, never a ministry, government department or the European Commission, and a source states that its staff are the host's employees, are assigned or seconded from the host or are hired through the host's own recruitment, or that an existing unit of the host was designated as the institute. Own staff: the institute employs people in posts of its own or recruits for them, including as a unit of a ministry, government department or the European Commission. Planned, when no current model is stated: adopted text, such as a cabinet decision or an adopted plan or strategy, sets up the staffing in the future. A proposal, such as a consultation draft, a budget proposal not yet voted or a bill, gives not published, with the proposal quoted in the notes with its source and date. Not published: searched and no source states it; a dated search log records each query, its language and the sources read. Where a newer official source contradicts an older one, the newer one decides and the notes record both. Notes also record secondments, concurrent posts, partners and contractors beside the main model. Not published means not stated in the sources searched, never that the institute has no staff.

Source preference: for a claim about a jurisdiction or its institute, cite that jurisdiction's own primary source first, in any language. Add an English-language source as a second citation where one exists, so readers can check it; it may come from another jurisdiction and does not replace the domestic primary source. Rely on an account from another country alone only when no source from the jurisdiction itself was found, and name who reported the claim in its description. Source origin identifies the issuer's country or international body, not the language or hosting server. Unknown origin is left null and reported for review, as are records with no citation from the jurisdiction itself.

Source titles: preserve the recorded original title. Add a faithful English translation when the title is non-English, including mixed-language titles; omit it for titles already in English and for proper names or acronyms alone. Source language describes the document read, not necessarily its title. A translation adds no dates, legal status or other claims absent from the original and is not presented as an official English title unless verified.
Consistency checks: where the same date or figure appears in several records, a check confirms it matches everywhere; it does not test whether the source is right.
Quotation checks: each quotation is matched word for word against our saved copy of its source; whether it supports the claim is judged in review.

Private evidence copies are kept for verification outside the repository. Complete HTML responses or PDF bytes are saved with the retrieval timestamp; rendered text from a third-party reader service is used when the original content is unavailable. Complete cited office documents and data archives are also preserved. Published source snapshot metadata contains only the retrieval timestamp, the SHA-256 checksum of the copy and, when the copy has text, a versioned hash of its normalised main text, never the copies or private paths. A later retrieval replaces the copy only when a quotation bound to the source that the cited copy carries no longer matches the new copy, when the new copy carries one the cited copy lacks, or when the cited copy is no longer held; for a source without bound quotations, only when its main text changed or cannot be compared. Other changes are reported for review and keep the cited copy. Public archive links use Wayback, with archive.today (archive.ph) as a fallback when a usable capture is found. Login, error and empty archive pages are rejected; unavailable sources remain explicit access limitations. We save a copy of each source as we read it; the copy shows what the source said, not that it is true. A Wayback viewer is checked through its raw document replay before judging the capture. New or replaced public archive links must match the recorded source URL or a documented redirect and have substantive matching content. A www host variant may be accepted without a recorded redirect only when its validated document bytes exactly match the original. Existing declared links that cannot be verified are retained with reported limitations, without claiming that their target or content has been verified. Demonstrated wrong-document, login or error captures are removed. Retrieval timestamps preserve their recorded precision and UTC offset.

Closest candidate: a jurisdiction with no institute identified may record one body with a model-level evaluation, testing or safety role, or a self-described qualifying function. Certification, performance testing and protection of AI models against attacks can meet this narrower related-body filter without qualifying for institute status. Stage describes the body, not jurisdiction status; pending extensions to an existing body are stated in its note. The gap is remit when a government act creates, plans, proposes or recognises the body but does not give it a qualifying role, and designation when the body does qualifying work, self-described or documented, without a government act concerning it. When both apply, remit takes precedence. The note states the evidence and its limits. Other related bodies are not recorded in this field.

None identified entries. Each state was searched in English and its official languages for a government-designated institute that evaluates advanced models; the entry names the languages searched. The bodies it lists never count as institutes: the closest candidate, AI Act authorities grouped by function, and other bodies. English names are our own faithful translations unless the body publishes its own English name, with the original beneath. The European Commission's contact list of 7 September 2026 marks some AI Act authorities as pending final adoption; for those states the national sources cited give the actual designation status.

Currency and rounding: Budgets published in other currencies are converted to euros at the ECB's annual-average rates for 2025, without inflation or purchasing-power adjustment; budget and staff figures are shown at two significant figures, and ~ marks a figure that is converted or changed by rounding, except the medians in the counts row, with the exact values in the downloads.

Budget display: every funding record states whether it covers the whole institute, a component or funding that is not institute-specific. Use the comparable whole-institute annual figure selected under Annual funding for both cards and the funding comparison. If none qualifies, use the latest adopted or announced whole-institute funding amount, including one-off and multi-year allocations; if there is none, use the latest whole-institute proposal. Exclude only records whose decision date lies wholly after the dataset date; an allocation already announced for a future funding period remains eligible. Rank eligible records by decision date when published, otherwise by the end of the sourced funding period, newest first; records with neither date follow those with one. Components and records without an amount cannot supply this fallback. Show the value first and its period, commitment and scope qualifications below. If no own funding qualifies, show Not published. An institute with own funding but no compared figure is listed below the funding comparison with its Budget value. Parent-body, host-programme, wider-ministry and broader-purpose amounts, including a body's funding before its designation, appear only as separately labelled Related funding, and remain in downloads.

Budget ratios: per person and share of GDP are computed only for the annual figure compared under Annual funding, and only for states; the EU and institutes without a compared figure have none. Per person divides that figure in euros by the state's population as recorded (see the population rules). Share of GDP divides it by the World Bank's GDP in current national currency for 2025, the year of the exchange rates; when the budget is in that currency no exchange rate enters, otherwise both are converted at the ECB 2025 rates. Both are computed from unrounded amounts and keep the figure's qualifier: an upper bound stays an upper bound and rounds up. They scale the figure and do not adjust it for purchasing power or for differences in what the figure covers. The denominators are for 2025, while the compared figure is for a funding period overlapping the reference year, which may be a fiscal year, a current-year allocation or a multi-year mean. The median annual budget in the counts row is taken over the compared figures as stated; when any of them is an upper bound, the median is an upper bound too, shown with "up to" and rounded up.

status_definitions.established: The government has created or designated a national body to evaluate the capabilities or risks of advanced AI models, or named a body as its AI safety or security institute.
status_definitions.planned: The government has adopted a commitment to create or designate a named national body to evaluate the capabilities or risks of advanced AI models or act as its AI safety or security institute.
status_definitions.proposed: The government has formally proposed a national body to evaluate the capabilities or risks of advanced AI models or act as its AI safety or security institute, but approval is pending.
status_definitions.exploring: The government is studying or drafting plans for a national body to evaluate the capabilities or risks of advanced AI models or act as its AI safety or security institute, or a government-appointed advisory commission has recommended one.
status_definitions.none_identified: Our searches found no current government decision, commitment, formal proposal, study, draft plan or government-appointed advisory recommendation for a national body to evaluate the capabilities or risks of advanced AI models or act as its AI safety or security institute.

in_house.label: Tests in house
in_house.definition: A source reports testing or evaluation of AI models that the institute itself has carried out or is carrying out, with its own staff or facilities. A statement of role or focus does not count. For a federation, only testing that a source attributes to the institute counts.

via_other_bodies.label: Testing by other bodies
via_other_bodies.definition: A source states that a named body outside the institute, such as a contractor or partner lab, tests or evaluates models for it.

planned.label: Testing planned
planned.definition: Adopted text, not a proposal, sets up testing capacity in the future.

not_published.label: Not published
not_published.definition: Searched; no source found states it. The dated search log is recorded with the value.

recent_access.label: Yes
recent_access.definition: The latest recorded access event falls within the twelve months up to the data date.

earlier_access.label: Yes, evidence from <year>
earlier_access.definition: Access events are recorded, the latest more than twelve months before the data date; the label gives its year.

by_law.label: By law
by_law.definition: No access event is recorded, but an operative legal provision gives the institute a power to require access to models.

access_agreed.label: Access agreed
access_agreed.definition: No access event or legal power is recorded, but a developer with a frontier model has published an agreement with the institute that provides for access to, or evaluation of, its models.

none_found.label: None found
none_found.definition: Searched; no source found records access, a legal power or an agreement. The dated search log is recorded with the value.

own_staff.label: Own staff
own_staff.definition: A source states that the institute employs people in posts of its own or recruits for them, including as a unit of a ministry, government department or the European Commission.

member_bodies.label: Staff of existing bodies
member_bodies.definition: The institute is a federation of existing bodies, and a source states that their staff do its work.

core_with_partners.label: Core team with partners
core_with_partners.definition: A source states that partner institutions do the institute's research or testing under its programme, and any central team of its own only coordinates, sets policy or represents it.

host_unit.label: Unit in a host body
host_unit.definition: The institute is a unit of an agency, public research body or university, and a source states that its staff are the host's, are hired through the host's recruitment, or that an existing unit of the host was designated as the institute.

planned.label: Planned
planned.definition: Adopted text, not a proposal, sets up the staffing in the future.

not_published.label: Not published
not_published.definition: Searched; no source found states it. The dated search log is recorded with the value.

membership_body.intl-network: International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (until December 2025: International Network of AI Safety Institutes). Members are countries and the EU; the member list is complete, so a jurisdiction without this entry is not a member.

timeline_event.proposed: An act meeting the proposed rung of the ladder in dataset.method. Implies proposed.
timeline_event.commitment: An act meeting the planned rung of the ladder in dataset.method. Implies planned.
timeline_event.designated: An act meeting the established rung of the ladder in dataset.method. Implies established.

timeline_event.first_output: Earliest identified publication credited to the institute by name, including guidance and named network contributions. No status effect.
timeline_event.withdrawn: Withdraws the earlier event named in 'withdraws'; status is recomputed from the surviving events.
timeline_event.closed: The institute is wound up; status returns to none_identified unless a later event applies.
timeline_event.mandate_changed: The institute mandate changes without establishing or closing it. No status effect.
timeline_event.named: A name for the institute or a documented predecessor comes into use where no other recorded event gives it. No status effect.

method_summaries.title: What counts as an institute
method_summaries.summary: We count a body as an AI Security Institute (AISI) if a national government, or the EU, has tasked it with testing general-purpose or frontier AI models for their capabilities and risks, or has named it its AI safety institute or its AI security institute. A regulator, certification body or cyber security agency does not count for that role alone.

method_summaries.title: Why this bar
method_summaries.summary: Evaluating advanced AI models distinguishes an institute from an AI regulator or digital ministry. Budgets and staff differ too much between countries for a size threshold, so we report them separately.

method_summaries.title: Population and regions
method_summaries.summary: Population comes from Eurostat for the 32 European states, the World Bank for the rest and Taiwan's Ministry of the Interior for Taiwan. Regions follow the UN's M49 grouping, with Taiwan placed in Eastern Asia.

method_summaries.title: Missing values
method_summaries.summary: An empty value means not known or not published. It never means zero or no.

method_summaries.title: Known activity
method_summaries.summary: Known activity, shown only for established institutes and separately from status, gives the earliest published evaluation or other technical work credited to the institute by name and the earliest joint testing it took part in. Finding none is not evidence of inactivity.

method_summaries.title: Check dates
method_summaries.summary: A check date records a full re-check against the sources. Where the original log is lost, it gives the latest day by which the check happened, which may be later than the check itself.

method_summaries.title: Status confidence
method_summaries.summary: Confidence describes the strength of the evidence for a status. None identified is a finding of our searches, not proof that nothing exists.

method_summaries.title: Quotations
method_summaries.summary: Key claims are backed by short quotations from their sources, with our English translations where needed. Review checks whether the quotations support the claims.

method_summaries.title: Outputs
method_summaries.summary: An output counts when the institute wrote it or is credited with it as its own work, with versions of one document counted once. Its first output is the earliest item credited to it, including network reports that name it.

method_summaries.title: Intervals between milestones
method_summaries.summary: We count the days from a government's first announcement or proposal to the institute's establishment, and from establishment to the first documented qualifying work credited to it. A date known only to the month or year gives a range, which stays in the downloads. The intervals are not a ranking, because the announcing act and the kind of body differ between states.

method_summaries.title: Agreements
method_summaries.summary: An agreement counts when the institute is a named party or a government agreement names it as the body carrying it out. Company pledges are recorded separately from signed agreements.

method_summaries.title: Budgets
method_summaries.summary: A card shows the institute's own funding for the year that includes the data date, otherwise the latest adopted or announced amount, and failing that the latest proposal. The chart compares adopted or announced whole-institute funding for a year overlapping the data year, while wider funding is shown as Related funding.

method_summaries.title: AI Act authorities
method_summaries.summary: Where a national act in force differs from the European Commission's list, we follow the national act. A pending proposal is not a designation.

method_summaries.title: Sources
method_summaries.summary: For a claim about a state or its institute we cite that state's own primary source first, in any language, and add an English source where one exists. Where we found only another country's account, the entry says who reported it.

method_summaries.title: Source titles
method_summaries.summary: Non-English source titles are kept in the original, with our English translation beside them. The translation adds no facts of its own and is not an official title.

method_summaries.title: Closest candidate
method_summaries.summary: For a state with no institute, the entry may name the one body that comes closest. It explains which government designation or qualifying role is missing.

method_summaries.title: None identified entries
method_summaries.summary: Each state was searched in English and its official languages for a government-designated institute that evaluates advanced models. Bodies listed for context never count as institutes.

method_summaries.title: Currency and rounding
method_summaries.summary: Budgets in other currencies are converted to euros at the ECB's 2025 average rates, with no adjustment for inflation or purchasing power. Budget and staff figures are rounded to two significant figures, and ~ marks converted figures and figures changed by rounding, except the medians.

method_summaries.title: Leadership
method_summaries.summary: We name a head when an official channel of the institute, its host or its government names that person in the role. This includes government directories and official social accounts. Press reports alone do not qualify. Otherwise the row reads Not published. A historical appointment or signature does not by itself confirm continuing tenure.

method_summaries.title: Reporting line
method_summaries.summary: We show the government body or bodies named as directing or overseeing the institute. This may differ from the organisation that hosts its staff. Joint oversight is shown together. The row does not imply independence, a direct reporting relationship to a minister, or that the host's director also leads the institute.

method_summaries.title: National partners
method_summaries.summary: We list public bodies and public-interest research organisations named by an institute or its government as working with it. A text in force that assigns the body a specific task counts as working with the institute; plans, strategies and future commitments are marked planned. An adopted programme for the current period that assigns the work counts as in force. A body mentioned only as an example in a general duty to cooperate is excluded. Consortium members need separate evidence to be listed individually. Hosts and private firms are excluded. Federation members are labelled members.

method_summaries.title: Testing and access
method_summaries.summary: We record whether a source says an institute tests AI models itself or through other bodies, and how it gets access to leading developers' models: dated access before public release or deeper access (fewer safeguards, or weights or internals), a legal power to require access, or a published agreement with a developer. Not published means not stated in the sources we searched.

related_bodies.name: Agencia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (ANIA)
related_bodies.role: Promotion and light-touch supervision body: registry, standards, sandbox, voluntary and mandatory registration; does not itself test models, so not counted.

jurisdictions.notes: Borderline case, kept as none identified. The agency (ANIA, created by Legislative Decree 234 of 26 February 2025 and now a decentralised public body) has a division for technical standards, risk frameworks and safety criteria, a voluntary registry with legal safeguards, a mandatory registry for consequential decisions in health, finance, public biometrics and public services, and a supervised sandbox. Its Resolution 0001/2025 (primary, read in full as text) says compliance checks focus on confirming that controls exist 'rather than a detailed technical review' (Art. 17) and that algorithmic impact assessments are done by the operators (Art. 15). No testing or evaluation of AI models by the agency is provided for. The law text itself (Decree 234) was not read; its description comes from the resolution and a press report. Resolution 0001/2025 Art. 19 prohibits requiring disclosure of source code, model architecture, weights or training data and bars mandatory third-party audits of these, and Art. 12(a) exempts providers of models, APIs and cloud services from mandatory registration on that basis alone; Art. 19 also limits ANIA to requesting high-level system descriptions, statistical summaries, performance metrics, dataset hashes and compliance statements; so ANIA cannot review models.

next_check.reason: Check whether ANIA starts evaluating or certifying models directly.

related_bodies.role: Regulator envisaged in articles 61–62 of the ministry's draft AI law, to be established by separate regulation. Would organise AI product and service risk assessments and supervise compliance; general-purpose AI developers would separately conduct and report evaluations under article 56. jurisdictions.notes: The ministry published its September 2025 draft for public consultation. Article 56 would place regular general-purpose AI evaluations on developers, who would report results to the competent authority. Articles 61–62 provide for a regulator to be established by separate regulation, including organising risk assessments of AI products and services. Articles 64–66 cover third-party evaluations, safety certification and risk monitoring. Article 58(2)(e) envisages AI evaluation services for society, while article 63(2) would give the authority evaluation mechanisms and adjustment of classification standards. The draft places general-purpose model evaluation on developers. It gives the regulator compliance and broad evaluation-service powers without specifying a qualifying model class and capability or behaviour-risk function. The scope of these powers requires clarification; no qualifying assignment was identified in the retrieved text. No later enactment or qualifying institute act was found in Portuguese and English searches. Separately, INACOM's primary account confirms that the March 2026 UNESCO readiness project aims to strengthen national AI governance; it does not describe a study of creating an AISI.

next_check.reason: Check enactment of the draft AI law and any regulation constituting its competent authority; reassess if a body receives a remit to evaluate advanced models for capabilities or behaviour risks.

model_access.notes: Event dates are the model's public release date in Epoch AI's data unless the source dates the access itself; the sources state that the access came before release, so the access took place on or before that date. The Epoch AI models cited for the leading-developer test were released at least a month before each such date. Not counted: Kimi K3 (Moonshot, July 2026), as Moonshot has never had a model in Epoch AI's frontier set and the access route is not stated; the Llama 3.1-405B network pilot (October to November 2024), as its weights are public. The developer agreements are the commitments of Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI to give the institute's predecessor 'deep model access', announced in 2023. No statutory power: no AI bill has been laid.

testing_capacity.notes: Testing reported, 2025-07-17: the AI Office ran the agentic evaluations for the cybersecurity strand of the network's joint testing; no AI Office evaluation of a named provider model was found. External evaluation support was procured under EC-CNECT/2025/OP/0032: lots 1 to 5 (CBRN, cyber offence, loss of control, harmful manipulation and sociotechnical risks) include ad hoc evaluations of general-purpose AI models chosen by the AI Office, and lot 6 builds an agentic evaluation interface for it. The award notice (OJ S 249/2025, 26 December 2025) lists the contractors by lot: lot 1 FAR AI, SecureBio and SaferAI; lot 2 Capgemini Consulting, Wavestone and the Laboratoire national de métrologie et d'essais; lot 3 EquiStamp, Model Evaluation and Threat Research and Epoch Artificial Intelligence; lot 4 EquiStamp, Clarity AI Research and the Centre pour la Sécurité de l'IA; lot 5 Technopolis Consulting Group Belgium, WIK-Consult and TNO; lot 6 the French ministry responsible for the budget and the Laboratoire national de métrologie et d'essais. No completed contractor evaluation has been published.

legal_power.conditions: Only for an evaluation under Article 92(1), which the AI Office conducts after consulting the Board, to assess a provider's compliance where information gathered under Article 91 is insufficient or to investigate systemic risks at Union level of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk; the request states its legal basis, purpose and reasons and the period for access, and the provider must provide the access requested.

model_access.notes: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1755 sets the arrangements: the access 'shall be appropriate to the objectives of the evaluation' and may include access through APIs, internal access, source code and model weights. No use of the power was found, and no access given to the AI Office by a developer was found; the network joint testing used open-weight models. Signing the general-purpose AI Code of Practice is not counted as an access agreement. Whether the evaluation contractors get privileged access is unknown: the tender specifications make the contractor responsible for 'the API costs associated with the GPAI model' and say 'Where not feasible, the AI Office shall aim to provide the required access.'

model_access.notes: Event dates are the model's public release date in Epoch AI's data unless the source dates the access itself; the sources state that the access came before release, so the access took place on or before that date. The Epoch AI models cited for the leading-developer test were released at least a month before each such date. NIST's release of 5 May 2026 says 'developers frequently provide CAISI with models that have reduced or removed safeguards' and that the institute 'has completed more than 40 such evaluations, including on state-of-the-art models that remain unreleased'; it names no model or developer for this access, so it is not a dated event. Not counted: GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, September 2026) and Kimi K3 (Moonshot, July 2026), assessed after public release with no access route stated; the June 2024 Claude 3.5 Sonnet testing, which the UK institute ran and 'shared their results with the US AI Safety Institute'; the Llama 3.1-405B network pilot, whose weights are public; and Claude Opus 5.5 (September 2026), whose system card says Anthropic 'collaborated with the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)' on measurement without stating pre-release access. Microsoft has had no model in Epoch AI's frontier set released since 1 January 2023; its latest there is Megatron-Turing NLG 530B (2021, with Nvidia). No legal power: Executive Order 14434 has no access provision for the institute.

national_partners.notes: Cyber agency searched: NCO (National Cybersecurity Office, 国家サイバー統括室), 2026-10-19 (ja, en); none found. NCO is listed among the relevant ministries and agencies in the J-AISI structure (deck, JP and EN) with no task assigned with the institute, so it is not an entry; the same applies to the other listed ministries and agencies. Fetches: aisi.go.jp top, about, partnership page + agreement PDF, JP and EN decks, cyber.go.jp top/about/overview/organize. No bilateral AISI-NCO instrument or joint output found; JPCERT/CC (roster suggestion) not found in any fetched AISI document. Deck footnote on the structure slide reads "＊2025年4月時点" (as of April 2025), so the member list may be older than the July 2026 deck date.

testing_capacity.notes: The institute's evaluation note of 2 October 2026 reports its own cyber capability evaluation of Claude Opus 4.8, carried out in June 2026. An older Cabinet Office draft of 7 April 2026 said: '主要国AISIのように、技術評価のR＆Dリソース・体制が十分になく、自らAI評価ツールを作ったり、評価することができていない。' (unlike major countries' institutes, it lacks sufficient R&D resources and structures for technical evaluation, and has not been able to build AI evaluation tools or carry out evaluations itself) and '現在は、パートナー協定を結んでいる国研（NICT、産総研、NII、理研、IPA等）の成果を活用するのみ。最近、民間企業への外注を開始。' (at present it only uses the outputs of the national research institutes with which it has partnership agreements, such as NICT, AIST, NII, RIKEN and IPA, and it recently began outsourcing to private companies); the newer statement decides. The Cabinet-decided AI Basic Plan of July 2026 sets out a stronger evaluation role. Joint network testing reported, 2025-06-26 (multilingual exercise: 'Australia and Japan also ran independent tests in Mandarin Chinese and Japanese') and 2025-07-17 (agentic exercise).

model_access.notes: The June 2026 evaluation of Claude Opus 4.8 ran with the real-time cyber safeguards normally applied in deployment removed; the note does not say how that access was provided. No legal power, and no agreement providing for access to or evaluation of a frontier developer's models, was found. Agreements with such developers provide for neither access to nor evaluation of their models: the Anthropic memorandum of cooperation (29 October 2025) is 'an agreement to conduct the exchange of information and best practices on methods for companies to evaluate capabilities, limitations, and risks of AI models', and the OpenAI memorandum (29 May 2026) only explores cooperation on safety evaluation and benchmarks. Anthropic's announcement of 31 March 2026 refers to 'the arrangements we have with safety institutes in the US, UK, and Japan, where early access and technical information sharing has helped governments', which is undated and names no model. The AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025) does not mention the institute.

national_partners.notes: Cyber agency searched: KISA (Korea Internet & Security Agency); NIS National Cyber Security Center as second, 2026-10-19 (ko, en); none found. No AISI-KISA or AISI-NIS relation published in any fetched document. Fetched: AISI English site (home, leadership, vision, organisation, policy, assessment, research, collaboration pages), AISI Korean home, KISA English and Korean homepages (200; no AISI mention found by title/menu scan, KISA about page /EN/about/sub01 returned 404), NIS homepage (200, JS shell with no text), plus one web search (ko, en) that returned only KISA-MSIT AI-security business programmes (2026-05) and no AISI link. The AISI policy page names "national security risk response" and "AI-induced vulnerabilities in national infrastructure" as tasks but names no cyber body; the AISI research page lists cybersecurity research only as a topic. The MSIT-Anthropic MOU (held kr-msit-anthropic-2026) is on AI safety and cybersecurity but names no cyber agency. Recorded as not published for the cyber domain, not as absence of any link.

testing_capacity.notes: Kakao says it carried out a joint safety evaluation of its own language model with the institute in 2025: '카카오는 지난해 인공지능안전연구소와 함께 자체 언어모델 'Kanana-1.5-9.8B'를 대상으로 공동 안전성 평가를 진행했으며' (last year Kakao, together with the AI Safety Institute, carried out a joint safety evaluation of its own language model Kanana-1.5-9.8B). Article 10(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the AI Basic Act lists '인공지능안전 관련 평가 시스템의 구축 및 운영' (building and operating AI safety evaluation systems) among the institute's tasks. Joint network testing reported, 2025-06-26 (multilingual exercise) and 2025-07-17 (agentic exercise).

model_access.notes: No access event, legal power or agreement providing for access to, or evaluation of, the models of a developer that has a model in Epoch AI's frontier set was found. Access to a model outside Epoch AI's frontier set: Kakao, which has never had a model in that set, jointly evaluated Kanana-1.5-9.8B with the institute in 2025 (access type not stated), and under the MOU of 28 September 2026 '카카오는 AI 안전성 평가 대상이 되는 자사 AI 모델과 AI 에이전트를 제공하고' (Kakao provides its own AI models and AI agents to be evaluated for AI safety), starting with pre- and post-deployment evaluation of language models. The OpenAI agreement (17 June 2026) shares evaluation methods and benchmarks and provides for neither access to nor evaluation of OpenAI's models; the Anthropic MOU (announced 29 June 2026, signing date not stated) is the science ministry's agreement, under which the institute is to cooperate, not an agreement between the institute and Anthropic. The bilateral agent evaluation with Singapore used models through public APIs. No legal power: the fact-finding powers of Article 40 of the AI Basic Act sit with the Minister of Science and ICT, and Article 10(3) of the Enforcement Decree lets the institute request materials only from state bodies.

Safety Institute (AISI)
The AISI can operate on a hub-and-spoke model
The recently established AI Safety Institute (AISI) should act as the main body responsible for guiding the safe and trusted development and use of AI in India.

The AISI should be involved in research, risk assessment, and capacity-building. It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and provide advice to policymakers and industry actors on issues of AI safety.
Develop draft guidelines, codes, standards, respective evaluation metrics and testing frameworks in collaboration with relevant agencies and sectoral regulators.
The AISI should also anchor India’s participation in global forums and facilitate collaborations, such as in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes.

excerpts.text: Building upon early access for recent codex models and gpt-5.2-thinking, both the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and the UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI) were granted early access to GPT-5.3-Codex.

sources.title: GPT-5.5 System Card

excerpts.text: We collaborated with the UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI) on pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities (and safeguards, see Section 9.3.2.7.1) for the launch of GPT-5.5.
UK AISI was provided access to a representative launch checkpoint and a checkpoint with reduced refusals for cyber capabilities.
We collaborated with the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) on pre-deployment testing of biological (and cyber, see Section 9.1.2.6) capabilities for the launch of GPT-5.5.
CAISI was provided access to a representative launch checkpoint and a checkpoint with reduced refusals for biological capabilities testing.

sources.title: GPT-6 Astra System Card

excerpts.text: To evaluate Astra’s alignment, UK AISI developed a new Out of Scope Supply Chain Attack evaluation based on recently observed cases of models engaging in supply-chain attacks on real open-source repositories.

sources.title: GPT-6 Astra performs unsanctioned supply-chain attacks in simulations

excerpts.text: Before its public release, AISI tested whether GPT-6 Astra would engage in this type of unsanctioned cyber activity when prompted to complete a cyber evaluation.

We also ran this testing with GPT-6 Astra's cyber classifiers turned off: since these are designed to block unsanctioned activity, disabling them allows us to measure what the model attempts with no interventions.

sources.title: Canada and Republic of Korea sign memorandum of understanding to advance AI innovation and safety
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
sources.access_note: Direct requests from the verification tool timed out on 24 October 2026; the excerpts were checked against a rendered text copy (r.jina.ai).

excerpts.text: The Canadian and Korean AI Safety Institutes
have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to strengthen international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) safety.
July 8, 2026

Under this agreement, the institutes will exchange information on AI technologies, risks, methodologies, tools and evaluations, as well as frameworks and guidelines related to the safe development and application of AI.
They will also work together to support internationally recognized and interoperable guidelines and standards for the evaluation of frontier AI technologies.
The two institutes will maintain regular consultations

changelog.summary: First public release. Each state's institute status and mandate, publications, funding, staff, leadership, national partners and source quotes, all downloadable as JSON and CSV.
changes: Covers all 193 UN member states plus Taiwan and the EU AI Office, with Europe in detail. For each state it records whether there is an institute, what it is meant to do, how it is set up, who it reports to and which national bodies it works with, with sources and the date on which each entry was last checked.

Lists each institute's publications and agreements, and shows its earliest published work and joint testing. When an institute was credited with a report later than the report appeared, both dates are shown.

Converts budgets to euros at the ECB's 2025 average rates and rounds them to two significant figures. The budget comparison counts only funding adopted or announced for the whole institute. Related funding and proposals are shown separately.
For states without an institute, says how sure we are. For some, it names the closest body and says why it does not count. AI Act authorities are listed separately from institutes.
Every claim cites its source, with source quotes and English translations of non-English source titles. Archive links are given where they exist.
Downloads in JSON and CSV, plus one file per state and per institute for scripts and agents.
Short method summaries on the page, with the full rules on a separate Method page. Figures from secondary sources, press reports or our own estimates are marked as such.
Code under MIT; data, page text and documentation under CC BY 4.0. Source quotes remain with their rights holders.

Records in the downloads and API whether a source states that an institute tests AI models, in house or through named other bodies, or plans to, and how it gets access to leading models: dated pre-release or deeper access, a legal power to require access, or an agreement with a developer that provides for access to, or evaluation of, its models, with quotations, Epoch AI's model data and dated search logs.

Gives the compared annual budget per person on the page, in the downloads and in the API, and its share of GDP in the downloads and API, using the recorded 2025 population and the World Bank's 2025 GDP in national currency.

Records how each institute is staffed (own staff, staff of existing bodies, a core team with partners, a unit in a host body, planned, or not published), each with a quotation from a source dated 2023 or later, in the downloads and the API.

changelog.summary: Corrections from a pre-launch accuracy check of the institute records, a re-check of 20 states with no institute identified, and clearer wording on the page.
changes: Japan: the institute now tests models itself. Its evaluation note of 2 October 2026 reports a June 2026 evaluation of Claude Opus 4.8 with the cyber safeguards removed, so testing reads In house and model access Yes. The note is added to its publications.

United States: earliest published work is now 17 January 2025, a technical blog on agent-hijacking evaluations by the institute's staff (then the U.S. AI Safety Institute), credited from the original version of the page.
Australia: earliest published work is now 10 August 2026, the institute's first publication, on risks and controls for multi-agent systems (research by Gradient Institute).
South Korea: staff of 38 as of October 2026, from a press report of the parliamentary audit; previously Not published.
Agreements added: the memorandum between the Canadian and Korean institutes of 8 July 2026, and the Korean institute's memorandum with Kakao of 28 September 2026.

National partners: entries that rested only on a list of participants or on past work, with no task assigned with the institute, are removed (Dstl in the United Kingdom, Viginum in France, eleven Japanese ministries and agencies, Nkom and the Data Protection Authority in Norway, which now reads Not published, and the Juvenile Prosecution Service in Spain).
Germany: the host is now the federation that the digital and interior ministries set up and task, as for France, so the member bodies are no longer also the host.
France: mandate texts now follow the founding announcement and the SGDSN page; the unsupported phrase on regulatory powers is removed.
Japan: the head's title is recorded as part-time, as published, and the staff target of 60 is attributed to the governing party's recommendation it comes from.
Malaysia: status confidence raised to high, because the ministry's release states the establishment.
EU AI Office: the staff record notes the lower figure on the AI Office's own page, and a note says the interval counts from the Commission decision of 24 January 2024.
Budgets: the US FY2026 note cites NIST's FY2027 request, which gives an existing CAISI base of USD 11m; the UK budget also cites the written answer of 15 October 2026.

Mandate and staff texts for the United Kingdom, Germany, Spain, Norway, the United States and South Korea reworded where they went beyond their sources, after a blind meaning check, with the supporting quotes bound.
Wording and source title corrections for Spain, Germany, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States.
Access notes record six cited pages whose live URLs now return 404 (among them NIST's May 2026 CAISI agreements announcement); their archived and retained copies remain the evidence.
Searched 20 states again for an institute that evaluates advanced models, in English and in national or official languages, with the limits recorded for Bhutan. None was found.

Raised confidence from low to medium for 13 of them (Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Egypt, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, Tunisia, United Arab Emirates), where primary sources on the national AI set-up are now cited; for Burkina Faso, French counts as a national or official language. The other 7 stay low, each with its reason recorded.

Page: the Network column says Not a member for states outside the international network instead of Not published; medium-confidence figures are labelled 'indirect or secondary'; a law is shown as the source of an institute's mandate ('mandate set by law').
Method: for budget and staff, Not published means that no figure was found in the sources checked.
Corrections: a report form on GitHub, prefilled from the page's correction links, and guidance for agents on answering from the data.
